structures.name: Oral cavity
structures.description: Boundaries include lips (anterior), cheeks (lateral), hard/soft palates (superior), floor of mouth (inferior); communicates posteriorly with oropharynx; pre-procedural inspection mitigates trauma, aspiration, and failed intubation risk.

structures.name: Nasal anatomy
structures.description: External bony/cartilaginous framework with nares; internal nasal cavity divided by septum; turbinates (inferior/middle/superior) along lateral walls; common pathologies include septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy, and polyps.

structures.name: Oropharynx
structures.description: Region behind oral cavity from soft palate to base of tongue; includes tonsils, base of tongue, soft palate; assessed by Mallampati classification.

structures.name: Hypopharynx
structures.description: Extends from hyoid to esophageal inlet; subdivided into piriform sinuses, postcricoid area, and posterior pharyngeal wall.

structures.name: Larynx
structures.description: Located C3–C6; mucosal folds (aryepiglottic, vestibular, true vocal folds), cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottic; paired arytenoid/corniculate/cuneiform), intrinsic and extrinsic muscles; glottis and subglottis as key regions.

structures.name: Trachea
structures.description: 10–11 cm long; internal diameter ~16–20 mm; supported by 16–20 C-shaped cartilages; posterior membranous wall comprises trachealis muscle; bifurcates at carina near sternal angle (T5).

structures.name: Tracheal blood supply
structures.description: Upper trachea from branches of inferior thyroid artery; lower trachea from bronchial arteries; venous drainage via superficial (azygous/accessory hemiazygous) and deep systems draining to pulmonary veins/left atrium.

structures.name: Endoscopic view of trachea
structures.description: Assess mucosal integrity, dynamic collapse (tracheomalacia/EDAC), extrinsic deviation; note tracheopathia osteochondroplastica sparing membranous wall.

structures.name: Main carina
structures.description: Sharp ridge separating right and left main bronchi; changes with respiration.

structures.name: Right bronchial tree
structures.description: Right main bronchus ~5 cm; gives RUL bronchus early; continues as bronchus intermedius to RML and RLL; segments: RUL (B1 apical, B2 posterior, B3 anterior); RML (B4 lateral, B5 medial); RLL (B6 superior, B7 medial basal, B8 anterior basal, B9 lateral basal, B10 posterior basal).

structures.name: Left bronchial tree
structures.description: Left main bronchus 4–5 cm under aortic arch; segments: LUL upper division (B1/2 apicoposterior, B3 anterior), lingula (B4 superior, B5 inferior), LLL (B6 superior, B7/8 anteromedial, B9 lateral basal, B10 posterior basal).

structures.name: Distal airways
structures.description: Bronchi transition to bronchioles as cartilage diminishes; terminal bronchioles within secondary lobules (Miller’s unit); respiratory bronchioles lead to alveolar ducts/sacs for gas exchange.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Mallampati classification
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Evaluate visibility of oropharyngeal structures and anticipate potential difficulties with airway access.
criteria_or_scoring: Class I: The soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar pillars are fully visible.
Class II: The soft palate and most of the uvula are visible.
Class III: Only the base of the uvula is visible, and the soft palate is partially visible.
Class IV: Only the hard palate is visible.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: The classification is based on the visibility of the soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar pillars when the patient opens their mouth and protrudes their tongue as much as possible, without phonation.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: To anticipate potential difficulties with airway access.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The Mallampati classification is a commonly used system used to evaluate the visibility of the structures in the oropharynx and to anticipate potential difficulties with airway access.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Axial CT interpretation of the larynx
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify laryngeal structures on CT and differentiate true versus false vocal cords; recognize subglottic region.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: On axial views of computed tomography of the larynx, the epiglottis is seen at the level of the hyoid cartilage and separates the vallecula from the laryngeal vestibule.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: The distinguishing feature between true and false vocal cords is fat in the false cords; the subglottic region is the narrowest part of the airway.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The distinguishing feature between true and false vocal cords is the presence of fat in the false vocal cords (Fig. 3d).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Endoscopic evaluation of trachea (bronchoscopy)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess tracheal mucosal integrity and identify extrinsic deviation or compression.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Starting at the upper trachea, mucosal integrity should be examined, even when there are no gross endobronchial lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Note extrinsic tracheal deviation and compression due to paratracheal masses.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The presence of extrinsic tracheal deviation and compression due to paratracheal masses should be noted.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Oral cavity inspection prior to airway procedures
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Ensure safety, reduce risk of complications, and guide differential diagnosis before procedures.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: An overall assessment of the oral cavity should be performed prior to procedures; inspect to ensure the cavity is clear and suitable.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Inspection ensures the oral cavity is clear and suitable for the intended procedure.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Prior to performing any type of procedure.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: An overall assessment of the oral cavity should be performed prior to performing any type of procedure.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Tongue mobility assessment for intubation difficulty
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Decreased tongue mobility (e.g., fixation) predicts failed intubation.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Decreased tongue mobility, such as a tongue fixation, is a predictor of failed intubation [4].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Jackson-Huber classification
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The nomenclature for bronchial anatomy consists of the Jackson-Huber classification and the Boyden surgical classification.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Boyden surgical classification
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The nomenclature for bronchial anatomy consists of the Jackson-Huber classification and the Boyden surgical classification.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Jackson–Huber classification of segmental airway anatomy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Classify segmental airway anatomy; named according to spatial orientation.
criteria_or_scoring: Named according to spatial orientation (anterior/posterior
superior/inferior
medial/lateral).
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Bronchoscopists commonly refer to bronchial anatomy using this system.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopists commonly refer to bronchial anatomy according to the Jackson-Huber classification of segmental airway anatomy (Table 1).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Yamashita Japanese nomenclature
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Alternative nomenclature for upper lobe anterior and posterior segments.
criteria_or_scoring: Assigns upper lobe anterior and posterior segments as listed in Table 1.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Less commonly adopted alternative to Jackson–Huber.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A less commonly adopted system is the Yamashita Japanese nomenclature [16], which assigns upper lobe anterior and posterior segments as listed in Table 1 and as shown in Fig. 5.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Boyden classification of bronchi
criteria_or_scoring: Refers to anterior and posterior segment of the left upper lobe as B2 and B3.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Preferred by thoracic surgeons and radiologists.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The Boyden classification refers to anterior and posterior segment of the left upper lobe as B2 and B3.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Inverted whale tail appearance on chest CT (RUL bronchus)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Imaging sign to identify RUL bronchus branch point and segmental origins.
criteria_or_scoring: Horizontal course of RUL bronchus with anterior and posterior segment origins.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: On chest CT, evaluate the RUL bronchus course and segmental origins.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Gives the inverted whale tail appearance.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: CT evaluation of right main bronchus/RUL branching.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The horizontal course of the RUL bronchus with origins of anterior and posterior segments gives the inverted whale tail appearance (Fig. 6b).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Apical segment circular lucency on CT
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Imaging feature to identify the apical segment.
criteria_or_scoring: At distal trachea level
apical segment appears as circular lucency near pulmonary vessels.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: On CT imaging at the level of the distal trachea, assess for circular lucency.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Circular lucency corresponds to apical segment.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: CT assessment of upper lobe segmental anatomy.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: On CT imaging, at the level of distal trachea, the apical segment appears as a circular lucency in proximity to pulmonary vessels.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Recognition of tracheal/accessory bronchus on CT (including bronchus suis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify bronchial variants that may explain imaging/clinical findings.
criteria_or_scoring: Tracheal/accessory bronchus arises immediately above main carina at right lateral aspect
called bronchus suis if it supplies entire upper lobe.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Assess CT scans near the main carina and right lateral aspect.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Variant bronchi identified; accessory bronchus may relate to recurrent/nonresolving infiltrate on radiograph.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When evaluating unexplained airway anatomy or recurrent infiltrates.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Sometimes, a tracheal bronchus or an accessory bronchus is noted on CT scans arising immediately above the main carina and at the right lateral aspect.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchus intermedius characteristics on chest CT
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Imaging identification of the bronchus intermedius.
criteria_or_scoring: Seen on several adjacent sections
oblique shape
courses posterior to right main pulmonary artery.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: On chest CT, review multiple adjacent sections for oblique airway posterior to right main pulmonary artery.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: CT interpretation of right-sided bronchial anatomy.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: On chest CT, the bronchus intermedius is characteristically seen on several adjacent sections.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Fish-mouth appearance of right middle lobe opening
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Visual sign suggesting extrinsic compression by interlobar lymph nodes.
criteria_or_scoring: Opening has a “fish-mouth” appearance due to extrinsic compression.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Appearance indicates extrinsic compression by interlobar lymph nodes.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When assessing the right middle lobe orifice.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Its opening may have a “fish-mouth” appearance due to extrinsic compression by interlobar lymph nodes.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Right carina nomenclature (RC1 and RC2)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Name carinal divisions between right lobar bronchi.
criteria_or_scoring: RC1 separates RUL orifice from bronchus intermedius
RC2 separates right middle and right lower lobes.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Use RC1/RC2 terminology to denote right-sided subcarinal landmarks.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The carina separating the right upper lobe orifice from the bronchus intermedius is right carina 1 or RC1.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Left carina nomenclature (LC1 and LC2)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Name subcarinal divisions on the left.
criteria_or_scoring: LC1 separates upper division of LUL and lingula
LC2 separates LUL and LLL.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Use LC1/LC2 terminology to denote left-sided subcarinal landmarks.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The subcarina separating the upper division of the left upper lobe and the lingula is left carina 1 or LC1.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopic recognition of tracheopathia osteochondroplastica
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify benign tracheal condition during bronchoscopy.
criteria_or_scoring: Nodular studding localizes to cartilaginous rings while sparing the membranous portion.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During bronchoscopic evaluation of the trachea.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: found incidentally, accounting for approximately two to seven per 1000 cases of bronchoscopies [14].

tables.title: Mucosal folds of the larynx
rows: Extend between the arytenoid cartilages and the lateral margins of the epiglottis, which in turn form the lateral borders of the laryngeal inlet. They are utilized in the closure mechanisms of the larynx.

Sit superior to the true vocal folds, these folds contain three distinct muscular systems. Below the vestibular folds are small cavities called ventricles that are bound inferiorly by the true vocal folds. The vestibular folds are involved in adduction and downward pressure, contributing in part to voice production.
The unique viscoelastic properties of these layers facilitate sound production and are critical for maintaining vocal fold pliability.

tables.title: Cartilaginous framework of the larynx
rows: Provides support for soft tissue structures. It is formed by two quadrilateral laminae that fuse anteriorly and inferiorly at an angle of 90° in men and 120° in women. This forms the laryngeal prominence and due to the sharper angle is more conspicuous in men and is commonly known as the Adam’s apple. It articulates with the cricoid cartilage below on the medial surface at the level just above the hyoid bone via the thyrohyoid and cricothyroid ligaments. This thin membrane is near the surface of the skin, relatively avascular, and serves as the landmark for an emergent cricothyroidotomy. On the external lateral surfaces, there are ridges connecting the extrinsic laryngeal muscles: the sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and inferior pharyngeal constrictor. The posterior margin of each thyroid lamina courses both upward and downward as superior and inferior cornua. The two superior horns suspend the larynx from the hyoid bone via lateral thyroid ligaments, and two inferior horns articulate with the cricoid cartilage.

Situated below the thyroid cartilage, this cartilage forms the only complete cartilaginous ring around the airway, with a narrow anterior arch and a broader posterior lamina. It articulates with the thyroid cartilage above by the median cricothyroid ligament and is attached to the first tracheal ring by the cricotracheal ligament. It supports the arytenoid cartilages.

These are paired, pyramid-shaped hyaline cartilages. They are positioned so that they sit on the superior border of the cricoid cartilage. They play a crucial role in vocal cord movement and phonation.

This leaf-shaped elastic fibrocartilage is located at the entrance of the larynx just distal to the base of the tongue. It is lined with mucous membrane and is attached to the arytenoid cartilages by the aryepiglottic folds laterally on both sides. The anterior aspect forms the inlet of the larynx. It functions to cover the glottis during swallowing, preventing food from entering the airway.
These small, conical cartilages sit atop the arytenoid cartilages and are involved in the movement and tension of the vocal cords.
These are small, rod-shaped cartilages located within the aryepiglottic folds, providing structural support to the laryngeal inlet and are paired with the corniculate cartilages.

tables.title: Trachea: extent and dimensions
rows: The adult trachea extends from the distal aspect of the cricoid cartilage, at the level of sixth cervical vertebrae, to the bifurcation at the main carina.
The trachea is approximately 10–11 cm in length, with an internal diameter of 16–20 mm [13].
The sagittal diameter is slightly longer than the coronal aspects, with the adult trachea measuring approximately 16 and 14 mm, respectively.

tables.title: Tracheal blood supply and venous drainage
rows: The blood supply of the trachea is derived from multiple sources, characterized by a complex network of arteries and anastomose [13].
Upper and lower trachea arterial supply
Branches of the inferior thyroid artery provide blood supply to the upper trachea and bronchial arteries supply the lower trachea (Fig. 5).
The bronchial arteries additionally supply blood to the esophagus via anastamosis with the inferior thyroid artery.
The posterior membranous wall of the trachea, however, receives some contribution from the esophageal arteries and their subdivisions.
Airway branches from main carina onward
From the main carina onward, subsequent airway branches derive their blood supply from three bronchial arteries: two branches supplying the left lung and one branch supplying the right lung.
The left bronchial artery originates from the descending aorta supplying the left lung.
The right lung airways have various alternative supplies, including the aorta, first or third intercostal arteries, internal mammary artery, or the right subclavian artery.

The venous drainage of the airways contains a superficial and a deep system. The superficial system receives blood from the bronchial vein system of the hilum and the visceral pleura, which leads to the azygous vein of the right lung and accessory hemiazygous vein of the left lung.
The deep venous system drains the deeper tributaries and then drains directly to the pulmonary vein or the left atrium.

tables.title: Laryngeal location and composition
rows: The larynx is situated in the anterior part of the neck, extending from the level of the third to the sixth cervical vertebrae (C3–C6).
It lies just below the pharynx and above the trachea.
The laryngeal apparatus is composed of mucosal folds, cartilages, muscles, and their respective neural innervations [6].

tables.title: Laryngeal muscle groups
rows: Working in pairs, the intrinsic muscles are primarily responsible for controlling the tension and position of the vocal cords while also controlling the degree of opening of the glottis. During expiration, speech, and deglutition, the adductor muscles reverse the process to close the glottis [12]. The tension of the vocal folds modulates airflow when they are adducted. The cricothyroid, vocalis, and thyroarytenoid muscles are responsible for tightening and relaxing the vocal folds for speech and phonation. These muscles are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, except the cricothyroid muscle, which is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

The extrinsic group consists of the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles and function to position the larynx within the neck and work to elevate or depress it during swallowing and phonation. They are further divided into elevators and depressors.

definitions.content: The oral cavity, also known as the mouth, is an anatomical structure that plays a crucial role in various functions such as speech, mastication, and swallowing. It is bounded anteriorly by the lips, laterally by the cheeks, superiorly by the hard and soft palates, and inferiorly by the floor of the mouth.

clinical_pearls.content: Occasionally, a nodular studding can be seen that localizes to the cartilaginous rings while sparing the membranous portion of the trachea. This benign condition, called tracheopathia osteochondroplastica, is usually asymp- tomatic and found incidentally, accounting for approximately two to seven per 1000 cases of bronchoscopies [14].

technology_and_technique.topic: Pre-procedure oral cavity assessment for bronchoscopy/intubation
technology_and_technique.summary: Systematic oral cavity inspection before airway procedures reduces risks of trauma, aspiration, and failed intubation. Specific safety points: mobile teeth can dislodge and obstruct the airway; the tongue can obstruct in sedated/comatose patients causing desaturation/hypoventilation; decreased tongue mobility is a predictor of failed intubation. Performance tips: mobilize the tongue (nondominant hand) to facilitate rigid bronchoscope passage; sweep the tongue laterally with direct laryngoscope during endotracheal intubation. No yield percentages provided.
technology_and_technique.reference: Patel S, Sung A, Frye L. Airway Anatomy. In: Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology. Springer; 2025. (refs [2], [4])

technology_and_technique.topic: Patient selection and aspiration risk clues from oral health
technology_and_technique.summary: Poor dental hygiene in high-risk patients (e.g., alcohol abuse) suggests aspiration risk with anaerobic infections and can correlate with air–fluid levels on imaging. Useful for selecting patients needing aspiration-focused diagnostics and preventive measures. No comparative effectiveness or yield data provided.
technology_and_technique.reference: Patel S, Sung A, Frye L. Airway Anatomy. In: Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology. Springer; 2025. (ref [3])

technology_and_technique.topic: Nasal route considerations for flexible bronchoscopy
technology_and_technique.summary: Nasal septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy, and nasal polyps are common anatomic barriers that can impact feasibility and safety of transnasal bronchoscopy. Selecting the passage with least resistance (and recognizing these variants) can reduce trauma and improve procedural success. No diagnostic yield or modality-comparison data provided.
technology_and_technique.reference: Patel S, Sung A, Frye L. Airway Anatomy. In: Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology. Springer; 2025. (ref [5])

technology_and_technique.topic: Role of bronchoscopy in lung cancer diagnosis and staging
technology_and_technique.summary: Bronchoscopy is routinely used to obtain specimens from lymph nodes, endobronchial lesions, and lung parenchyma to establish histologic diagnosis and determine stage. Precise anatomic localization informs candidacy for surgical resection versus medical therapy. The chapter does not provide yield percentages, safety rates, or comparative effectiveness versus other modalities.
technology_and_technique.reference: Patel S, Sung A, Frye L. Airway Anatomy. In: Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology. Springer; 2025. (ref [1])

points: 10 Abstract The human airway consists of the upper and lower air- ways
The larynx, being part of the upper airway, contrib- utes to phonation, respiration, and prevention of aspiration
Its anatomy plays a central role in the complex sensorimotor functions including swallowing and speech production
